experiment.elements-plus.group.intro.sec: Welcome to the ElementsPlus Experiment Table!
Here you can test your own circuits and gradually unlock various advanced components.
Insert your circuit diagram into the slot above and click the "Start Experiment" button, and the experiment will be automatically performed.

After the experiment is successful, you will obtain a compiled circuit diagram, which is associated with a component. It can be used directly as a component in the lithography machine, or used in the "Manufacture" tab of the lithography machine to manufacture chips.

Note: Compiled circuit diagrams cannot be edited further, but you can create a copy of the circuit diagram in the lithography machine manufacturing page, and uncheck the "Keep Compiled" option. The copy will no longer have the compiled status and can be edited further.

If the experiment fails, the progress bar will turn red, and hovering over it will show the specific failure reason. The state of the input components in the circuit diagram will be frozen at the failed test case, and you can view the specific failure logic by placing it in the lithography machine later.
That's all to be introduced, start your experiment journey now, have fun!
experiment.elements-plus.group.amplifier: Signals have 0~15 strengths in total, but we mostly focus on "yes" and "no".

To achieve this, we introduce a simple component - the %s. As long as the input signal strength is greater than 0, the output signal strength is 15. Thus, we can focus on higher-level logic without worrying about the details.
To achieve this, we need a component that can amplify the signal strength. And that is the %s.

A transistor is a component that can amplify signals. When there is no input on the side, it can amplify the input on the front by two times. (Side input will be mentioned later, this experiment does not require it)
Now, try to use this property to complete the experiment.
Input A, as long as A is non-zero, output Y=15, otherwise output Y=0.

Please build the circuit in the lithography machine, and place the circuit diagram into the slot above after completion. Click the "Start Experiment" button, and the experiment will be automatically performed.
You should see below the "Test Information" appear multiple boxes, each corresponding to a test case. The text above the test case means:
• %s: Test is still running (you will see in the sequential logic that will be introduced later)
experiment.elements-plus.group.first_gat: First Gate
Good job, you should now have passed your first experiment and obtained a compiled circuit diagram.
A compiled circuit diagram can be used directly as a component in the lithography machine design page, and you can also add it to the component list.
You should have already noticed the lithography machine manufacturing page, and it is now time to understand how to use it.
The lithography machine manufacturing page can copy circuits, manufacture chips and circuit boards.

If you want to copy a circuit, please place the circuit in the first slot as a template, and the second slot with the uncompiled circuit to be covered. At this time, a copy of the template circuit will appear in the output slot. Take it away, and the template will not be consumed, and the second slot circuit will be consumed. (Note: This operation will permanently cover the second slot circuit, and it is recommended to use an empty circuit)

If you want to make a chip, please place the compiled circuit diagram in the first grid as a template, and place the empty chip that %s in the second grid. At this time, the raw materials required for making the chip will be displayed.
greater than or equal to circuit diagram scale
Among them,
• Basic components usually need the corresponding amethyst component items
• Advanced components need corresponding chips of any scale (manufactured by this method)
• Wires need corresponding block number of %s and %s items (bus multiplied by bit width)
• Input/output and bus joiner/splitter does not require raw materials
When all raw materials are satisfied in the inventory, a chip will appear in the output slot. Take it away, and the empty chip and raw materials will be deducted.
Now that we have learned how to make chips, we will move on to making the first logic gate.

We have already introduced the amplification function of transistors, and now we introduce the side input of transistors. The side input will make the output linearly decay. 0 corresponds to 100% output, and 15 corresponds to 0% output (that is, completely shutting down the output).
If you are more comfortable using formulas, then in other words: the final output ratio of the transistor is %s. That is, the output is %s.
2*(1-side_input/15)
2*front_input*(1-side_input/15)

This time, we are going to design the component "%s". It is very simple——it has only one input and one output. You just need to ensure that it outputs 15 when the input is 0, and outputs 0 when the input is not 0.
NOT Gate
Hint: When the input is 0, the component cannot produce a signal out of thin air. Think of which basic component can produce a signal continuously?
In fact, with this component, you can create any complex %s.
combinational logic circuit

What we call a %s is a digital circuit whose output depends only on the current input state and not on the past state of the circuit. If you understand this, then congratulations, you still have some basic knowledge. If you find it difficult to understand, that's okay, you will gradually understand it later.
combinational logic circuit
If you think it's too simple, here's a challenge for you: design a component that outputs %s. We call it the "%s".
15-input
Analog NOT Gate
This experiment is optional, you can continue to the next chapter and come back to do it later.
experiment.elements-plus.group.basic_gat: Now that we have built our first logic gate, let's move on to building more logic gates.
This chapter's logic gates will no longer have only one input, but usually have A and B two inputs.
• %s: If any input is non-zero, it outputs 15, otherwise it outputs 0.
• %s: If both inputs are non-zero, it outputs 15, otherwise it outputs 0.
• %s: If any input is non-zero, it outputs 0, otherwise it outputs 15.
• %s: If both inputs are non-zero, it outputs 0, otherwise it outputs 15.
Hint: NOR gate and NAND gate are not always just OR gate and AND gate with an additional NOT gate. For example, NAND gate actually needs fewer transistors than AND gate.
In the following chapters, we will frequently use these basic logic gates.
Additionally, this chapter also has an optional challenge:
• %s: If A is non-zero, output B, otherwise output A
• %s: If A is zero, output B, otherwise output A
experiment.elements-plus.group.advanced_: I'm sure you're already intimidated by the high cost of batteries, but it's okay. You don't need or recommend having a built-in battery for every chip - the chips you want to manufacture in the future will require more and more sub chips, and this "built-in battery" design will undoubtedly increase costs exponentially.

The experiment table will provide an additional optional input, "VCC", which you can connect to any pin of your circuit, and it will automatically receive a signal strength of 15. The VCC pin will not be explicitly exposed on the component; they will be implicitly connected to the outer layer one by one, so you only need one battery to power the entire machine.
You can also follow the same design when designing circuits: do not built-in batteries, but reserve input interfaces instead, which can significantly reduce the demand for batteries!
After making the basic logic gates, let's move on to two more advanced logic gates. These gates also have A and B two inputs and Y one output.
• %s: Odd number of inputs non-zero, output 15; even number of inputs non-zero, output 0.
• %s: Odd number of inputs non-zero, output 0; even number of inputs non-zero, output 15.
You can try to solve it by combining the logic gates you have unlocked before.

After completing these chapters, you can directly jump to “%s”, but it is recommended that you complete these chapters as soon as possible, as they can provide a lot of help in your future design. Moreover, they are prerequisite chapters for some optional chapters.
experiment.elements-plus.group.three_way: We have already built some logic gates, and sometimes we need to handle data that is three or more. By connecting two components in series, we can achieve this, but we can also integrate it into a more efficient component.
In this experiment, we will build a three-way logic gate, which takes inputs A, B, and C, and produces an output Y:
• %s: If any one of the inputs is non-zero, it outputs 15, otherwise it outputs 0.
• %s: If all three inputs are non-zero, it outputs 15, otherwise it outputs 0.
• %s: If an odd number of inputs are non-zero, it outputs 15; if an even number of inputs are non-zero, it outputs 0.
• %s: If an odd number of inputs are non-zero, it outputs 0; if an even number of inputs are non-zero, it outputs 15.
This chapter is optional, you can choose to directly proceed to the next chapter, but completing this chapter first may be helpful for your future design.
experiment.elements-plus.group.multiplex: Multiplexer
%s can select one of multiple inputs as output, which is very helpful when designing Arithmetic Logic Unit.
Multiplexer

Note: Due to the complex logic of this circuit, it is difficult to preserve the signal strength. Therefore, the input D, D0, D1, D2, and D3 involved in the following experiment only consider two cases: 0 and non-zero. Non zero is considered as 15, rather than outputting the original signal strength. Below is referred to as "%s".
Amplified Value
Firstly, we have %s: Input A, D0, D1. When A is 0, output Y is the amplified value of D0. When A is non-zero, output Y is the amplified value of D1.
2-to-1 Multiplexer
If you still don't know how to do it, think about what component in the %s we did earlier has the most similar function to a "switch"?
Basic Gate
Then we extend the input to 4 lines, and we have %s.
4-to-1 Multiplexer
Inputs A0, A1, D0, D1, D2, D3, Output Y.
• When A1 is 0 and A0 is 0, output D0's amplified value.
• When A1 is 0 and A0 is non-zero, output D1's amplified value.
• When A1 is non-zero and A0 is 0, output D2's amplified value.
• When A1 is non-zero and A0 is non-zero, output D3's amplified value.
Hint: Four-to-one, is equivalent to first four-to-two and then two-to-one.
Then we stack 8 lines, and we have %s. It can select %s.
8-to-1 Multiplexer
8-bit Bus
Not yet understand the concept of %s? You can complete “%s” chapter first before coming back.
Bus
Multi-bit Adder
The characteristics of 8-bit multiplexer are the same as 1-bit, just with input D0~D4 and output Y changed to %s.
8-bit

There is another useful component called “%s”, which acts similarly to a switch, only outputting a signal when “enabled”, otherwise outputting 0. Therefore, through this component, multiple data outputs can be easily connected to a shared bus, as long as only one is valid at any time to avoid data interference. Although the 8-bit operation corresponding to the components at the beginning can also be achieved, it is slightly more tedious. Encapsulating it into a single component can simplify the logic.
8-bit Tri-state Buffer
It has two inputs: enable input A and data input D, one output Y. Where D and Y are both %s. When A is non-zero, output Y as the amplified value of D; When A is 0, the output Y is all 0.
8-bit
Another option is to try the "%1$s". This is left as an optional experiment for you. Completing the optional experiments "%3$s" and "%4$s" in "%2$s" chapter may make it easier.
Analog Multiplexer
Basic Gate
Short-circuit AND
Short-circuit OR
experiment.elements-plus.group.encoder_d: Not yet familiar with the concept of binary? You can complete the “%s” chapter first before coming back.

There is a component that lights up a separate output line for each binary input, which is the %s. Its reverse operation: outputting the lit input line as the corresponding binary number, which is the %s.
All decoder logic can be generalized as:

Inputs A0~An, outputs Y0~Ym %s. Only one output is 15, and the rest are all 0. According to the two states of the inputs, 0 and non-zero, corresponding to 0 and 1 respectively, they form the binary number x=(An...A2A1A0)₂. Which output is 15 depends on x; only Yx outputs 15.
To save component space, we pack the outputs into %s. The upper Y0~Y7 correspond to bits 1~8 of the following Y or Y0 respectively, and Y8~Y15 correspond to bits 1~8 of Y1.
• %s (Optional): Inputs A0~A3, outputs Y0 (packed Y0~Y7), Y1 (packed Y8~Y15).
Then there is the encoder. The logic of the encoder is the opposite of the decoder, and can be generalized as:
Inputs A0~Am %s, outputs Y0~Yn. When an input is non-zero, output its binary representation (Yn...Y2Y1Y0)₂, where 0 corresponds to signal strength 0, and 1 corresponds to signal strength 15.

To avoid undefined behavior, we specify that if multiple inputs are non-zero at the same time, the output is the bitwise OR of the outputs corresponding to all non-zero inputs. For example, for an 8-3 encoder, when A5 (corresponding to output 101) and A6 (corresponding to output 110) are active at the same time, the output is 111. In practical applications, you should generally avoid multiple inputs being non-zero at the same time.
• %s (Optional): Inputs A0 (packed A0~A7), A1 (packed A8~A15), outputs Y0~Y3.
There is also one called the “%s”. Unlike a normal encoder, when multiple inputs are non-zero, only the largest input actually takes effect. This is an optional experiment.
experiment.elements-plus.group.one_bit_a: Have you ever wondered how we represent numbers in circuits?
Indeed, the signal strength of 0~15 can represent 16 numbers. However, signal strength also has its drawbacks: it is difficult to read and process, and it will attenuate in macro circuits.
To address this, we will introduce a more stable and easy-to-use number representation method——%s.

The numbers we use daily are base 10 (%s), which means we carry over every 10. Binary, on the other hand, is base 2, meaning each digit in a binary number can only be 0 or 1. When 1+1, it equals (10)₂. This way, we can represent a binary number using multiple wires, and we don't care about the signal strength of each digit, only whether it 'has' or 'does not have' a signal, corresponding to 1 and 0 respectively.
In this experiment, we will handle the addition of one-bit binary numbers. First, we need to do the addition of two one-bit binary numbers. This component is called the “%s”.
• %s: Inputs A and B, add A and B as binary numbers (non-zero corresponds to 1, zero corresponds to 0), output sum S and carry C (1 corresponds to 15, 0 corresponds to 0).
To make it more intuitive, we list all the cases of the half adder below:

Handling the addition of two one-bit binary numbers is not enough, because if we want to perform addition of multi-bit binary numbers, we need to handle the carry problem. Therefore, we need to handle the addition of three-bit binary numbers, which is called the “%s”.
• %s: Inputs A, B, and CI, add A and B as binary numbers (non-zero corresponds to 1, zero corresponds to 0), output sum S and carry CO (1 corresponds to 15, 0 corresponds to 0).

experiment.elements-plus.group.bitwise_o: A bitwise operator is a component that can perform some logical operation on a bus bit by bit. These include AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR and XNOR.
Except for the %s, they all have two 8-bit inputs A and B and one 8-bit output Y, and each bit performs the corresponding logical operation independently.
The %s has only one 8-bit input A and one 8-bit output Y, and each bit is inverted independently.

The operations above are performed on all bits in parallel. In addition, you may occasionally need judgements such as “any bit is non-zero” or “all bits are non-zero”, or need to know whether the number of non-zero bits is odd or even. Chaining multiple logic gates each time is troublesome, so here we also provide 8-way logic gate component experiments. These are optional; if you feel you don't need them, you can skip them.
These components all have one 8-bit input A and one 1-bit output Y.
• %s: If any input bit is non-zero, output 15; otherwise output 0.
• %s: Only when all input bits are non-zero at the same time, output 15; otherwise output 0.
• %s: If an odd number of input bits are non-zero, output 15; if an even number are non-zero, output 0.
• %s: If an odd number of input bits are non-zero, output 0; if an even number are non-zero, output 15.
experiment.elements-plus.group.multi_bit: Multi-bit Subtraction

Previously we learned to represent numbers in binary and to add binary numbers. In this chapter we will subtract multi-bit binary numbers. The most direct idea is, like the decimal column method, to subtract bit by bit from the low position to the high position, borrowing 1 from the next higher bit when needed. But computers are better at addition, and designing a separate subtraction circuit is not worthwhile. So we want to turn subtraction into addition as well: %s.
A − B = A + (−B)
The problem then becomes: with a fixed number of bits containing only 0 and 1, how do we represent a negative number? The answer is — %s.
two's complement

Take 8-bit binary as an example. There are 2^8=256 states in total, which we can view as a cycle “modulo 256”. The value -x is the number that satisfies %s while discarding the carry out of the highest bit; that number is 256-x.
Since %s, and 11111111-x is exactly the bitwise inversion of every bit of x, we get the core mnemonic of two's complement:
%s
Invert every bit, then add one to the last bit.
Note: all 8 bits must take part in the inversion; the +1 starts from the least significant bit and carries bit by bit; if the highest bit produces a 9th carry, it is simply discarded.
For example, to find the 8-bit two's complement of -10, the negation of +10:
• Bitwise inversion: 11110101
• Add one to the last bit: 11110110
So the 8-bit two's complement of -10 is 11110110. Verify: %s; discarding the carry out of the highest bit gives 00000000, which is exactly 0.

Conversely, if we invert 11110110 and add one again, we get back +10. This shows that the “invert and add one” of two's complement is reversible. The two's complement of a positive number is itself, and 0 has only one representation: 00000000.
With two's complement, multi-bit subtraction can be unified into multi-bit addition. To compute A-B:
1. Write both A and B as the same 8 bits;
2. Find the negation of B: invert all 8 bits of B, then add one to the last bit, to get -B;
3. Perform ordinary binary addition A + (-B), adding bit by bit and propagating carries, discarding the carry out of the highest bit;
4. The result is the two's complement of A-B.
For example, computing 12-5: %s, which gives 00000111, i.e. 7.

The range representable by 8-bit two's complement is -128 to +127. A highest bit of 0 indicates a positive number or 0, and a highest bit of 1 indicates a negative number. Going beyond this range causes overflow; for example, 127+1 gives 10000000, which reads as -128 in 8-bit two's complement, not +128.
In short, two's complement turns subtraction into addition: %s, where ~B means bitwise inversion.
In this experiment we will build the “%s”.
8-bit Negator
Input A (8-bit); output the two's complement representation of its negation Y (8-bit).
Combined with the %s, you can then implement 8-bit subtraction.
8-bit Adder
experiment.elements-plus.group.bitwise_s: Shifter
In the previous chapter we learned the concept of %s. From now on, “%s”, unless stated otherwise, always refers to two's complement.
two's complement
signed number

A shifter is a component that can shift a binary number left or right by some number of positions. For non-rotating shifts, shifting left by n is equivalent to multiplying by 2^n, and shifting right by n is equivalent to dividing by 2^n and rounding down; right-shifting a signed number requires an arithmetic right shift that preserves the sign bit.
For example, shifting 0000 1001 left by 3 gives 0100 1000.

Shift operations come in two kinds: %s and %s. Logical shifts do not distinguish the sign bit and always fill vacated bits with 0; arithmetic right shifts preserve the sign bit and fill vacated high bits with the sign bit. For left shifts the results are the same (low bits are filled with 0), so only a separate arithmetic right shifter is needed.
logical shift
arithmetic shift

The difference between logical and arithmetic right shift can be seen with 1001 0110: logical right shift by 3 gives 0001 0010, while arithmetic right shift by 3 gives 1111 0010 (the highest bit is 1, so vacated high bits are filled with 1).

To avoid overlapping functionality, the shifter is split by shift direction and fill rule into three unidirectional versions: %s, %s and %s. The bidirectional version is kept as an optional experiment.
8-bit Left Shifter
8-bit Right Shifter
8-bit Arithmetic Right Shifter
If A is a signed number, use the arithmetic right shifter when shifting right; a logical right shift treats the sign bit as ordinary data and may produce a large positive number.

Unidirectional shifters (including the later rotate and analog versions) use only the low 3 bits of B as the shift amount, so the amount is 0–7 and the high 5 bits of B are ignored. Non-rotating shifts by 8 or more move out all original bits, while rotations have a period of 8, so 3 bits are enough to represent every valid shift amount. For example, the low 3 bits of B=8 are 0, which is equivalent to no shift.

• %s: Inputs A (8-bit) and B (8-bit, only the low 3 bits are effective); output Y (8-bit) is A shifted left by B bits (0 maps to 0, 1 maps to 15); low bits are filled with 0 and bits shifted out of the high end are discarded.
8-bit Left Shifter
• %s: Same inputs as above; output Y is A logically shifted right by B bits; high bits are filled with 0 and bits shifted out of the low end are discarded.
8-bit Right Shifter

• %s: Same inputs as above; output Y is A arithmetically shifted right by B bits; high bits are filled with the sign bit (0 for positive, 1 for negative) and bits shifted out of the low end are discarded.
8-bit Arithmetic Right Shifter

The bidirectional versions do not use the low-3-bit rule. Instead, the whole 8-bit B represents both direction and amount as a signed number (two's complement): positive shifts left, negative shifts right.

• %s: Inputs A (8-bit) and B (8-bit); output Y (8-bit). When B is positive, Y is A shifted left by B bits; when B is negative, Y is A shifted right by |B| bits. Bits shifted out are discarded, and missing bits are filled with 0 (0 maps to 0, 1 maps to 15).
8-bit Shifter
• %s: Same inputs and outputs as above; the difference is that missing bits are filled with 0 on left shifts and with the sign bit on right shifts.
8-bit Arithmetic Shifter

There is also a %s, which does not discard bits shifted out but rotates them to the other side. For example, 1001 0110 rotated left by 6 becomes 1010 0101. Like ordinary shifters, the rotator is split into unidirectional left-rotate and right-rotate versions plus a bidirectional version. These are optional experiments.
rotator
• %s: Inputs A (8-bit) and B (8-bit, only the low 3 bits are effective); output Y is A %s rotated left by B bits (0 maps to 0, 1 maps to 15); bits shifted out of the high end wrap to the low end.
8-bit Left Rotator
circularly
• %s: Same inputs as above; output Y is A %s rotated right by B bits; bits shifted out of the low end wrap to the high end.
8-bit Right Rotator
circularly
• %s: Inputs A (8-bit) and B (8-bit); output Y (8-bit). Bidirectional version. The whole 8-bit B is treated as a signed number; positive rotates left, negative rotates right.
8-bit Rotator

There is also an %s, which preserves the signal strength of non-zero bits instead of turning them all into 15. For example, 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 shifted left by 4 becomes 5 6 7 8 0 0 0 0, and rotated left by 4 becomes 5 6 7 8 1 2 3 4. The analog shifter is split into unidirectional left-shift, right-shift, left-rotate and right-rotate versions, plus two bidirectional versions. These are optional experiments.
analog shifter
Each output bit of a digital shifter is either 0 or 15; an analog shifter preserves the original 0–15 signal strength.

• %s: Inputs A (8-bit) and B (8-bit, only the low 3 bits are effective); output Y is A shifted left by B bits, preserving each channel's signal strength; low bits are filled with 0 and bits shifted out of the high end are discarded.
8-bit Analog Left Shifter
• %s: Same inputs as above; output Y is A logically shifted right by B bits, preserving each channel's signal strength; high bits are filled with 0 and bits shifted out of the low end are discarded.
8-bit Analog Right Shifter

• %s: Inputs A (8-bit) and B (8-bit); output Y (8-bit). Bidirectional version. The whole 8-bit B is treated as a signed number; positive shifts left, negative shifts right (high bits are filled with 0); each channel's signal strength is preserved.
8-bit Analog Shifter

• %s: Inputs A (8-bit) and B (8-bit, only the low 3 bits are effective); output Y is A circularly shifted left by B bits, preserving each channel's signal strength; bits shifted out of the high end wrap to the low end.
8-bit Analog Left Rotator
• %s: Same inputs as above; output Y is A circularly shifted right by B bits, preserving each channel's signal strength; bits shifted out of the low end wrap to the high end.
8-bit Analog Right Rotator

• %s: Inputs A (8-bit) and B (8-bit); output Y (8-bit). Bidirectional rotate version. The whole 8-bit B is treated as a signed number; positive rotates left, negative rotates right; each channel's signal strength is preserved.
8-bit Analog Rotator
experiment.elements-plus.group.alu_basic: This is the last required experiment in the combinational-logic part. You have now learned some ways to operate on binary numbers. In a computer, we need to decide what operation to perform based on a stretch of binary bits in an instruction. That stretch of bits is called the “opcode”.
In this experiment we will build a circuit that implements 8 operations. The opcodes and their corresponding operations are as follows:
• %s: Bitwise logical left shift (%s) (only the low 3 bits of B are used as the shift amount)
• %s: Bitwise logical right shift (%s) (only the low 3 bits of B are used as the shift amount)

• %s: Inputs are two operands A (8-bit) and B (8-bit), an optional carry/borrow input CI (1-bit), and an opcode OP (8-bit, only the low 3 bits are valid). Output Y (8-bit) is the operation result, and CO (1-bit) is the optional carry/borrow output. Shift operations use only the low 3 bits of B as the shift amount.

CO is the carry output for addition; for subtraction it is the borrow output (1 when A<B+CI, meaning the subtraction underflows); for all other operations it is 0. CI acts as the borrow input for subtraction.
experiment.elements-plus.group.alu_advan: You have completed the %s and the %s; now you can give your ALU multiplication as well.
The advanced version uses a 4-bit opcode. 0000~0111 are the same as the basic version, 1000 is multiplication, and 1001~1111 are reserved:
• %s: Bitwise logical left shift (%s) (only the low 3 bits of B are used as the shift amount)
• %s: Bitwise logical right shift (%s) (only the low 3 bits of B are used as the shift amount)

• %s: Inputs are two operands A (8-bit) and B (8-bit), an optional carry/borrow input CI (1-bit), and an opcode OP (8-bit, only the low 4 bits are valid). Output Y0 (8-bit) is the operation result (the low 8 bits of a product), Y1 is the high 8 bits of a product (all 0 for other operations), and CO (1-bit) is the optional carry/borrow output. Shift operations use only the low 3 bits of B as the shift amount.

The CO convention is the same as the basic version: carry for addition; borrow for subtraction (1 when A<B+CI, meaning the subtraction underflows); 0 otherwise. CI acts as the borrow input for subtraction.
experiment.elements-plus.group.bus.secti: Before implementing multi-bit addition, let us introduce the concept of %s.
bus
A bus is a bundle of multiple wires, which simplifies wiring so you do not need to arrange multiple parallel wires.

The number on the right side of the wire button in the lithography machine tool bar is the current bit width. You can click or scroll the mouse wheel on it to switch the bit width. The bus will no longer change color according to the signal strength, but will display a fixed color corresponding to the bus bit width. Only wires with matching bit width can be connected to certain component pins.
Find “%s” and “%s”, as well as “%s” and “%s” in the component list. We will use them in this chapter.
8-bit Input
8-bit Output
8-bit Bus Joiner
8-bit Bus Splitter
We unify the rules for bus joiners and splitters, specifying that the side closer to the opposite pin (the upper side when placed upright) is the least significant bit.
In the following, “1-bit” and “8-bit” usually refer to the number of channels in a bus, or to the binary value formed by treating each channel as 0/1.
Try it:
• %s: No inputs; always outputs 8-bit Y=123 (a 0 bit corresponds to 0, a 1 bit to 15).
8-bit Constant
• %s: Input A (1-bit). When A is non-zero, outputs 8-bit Y=123 and each channel has the same signal strength as the input; otherwise outputs all zeros.
8-bit Mask

The constant 123 in the test cases is only used to check whether you understand the concept. Both components have configurable properties; select the component and set any value in the attribute panel on the right, or double-click the component to enter a number directly.
• %s: Input A (8-bit); output Y (1-bit) is bit 3 of A (bit 0 is the least significant bit), preserving signal strength.
8-bit Bit Extractor
• %s: Inputs A (8-bit) and B (8-bit). The low 3 bits of B represent a binary number (0–7); output Y (1-bit) is the amplified value of that bit of A (0 maps to 0, non-zero maps to 15).
8-bit Bit Indexer
The bit extractor always takes a fixed bit; the bit 3 used in the test cases is only for testing. You can configure which bit to extract (0–7) in the component settings.
In some analog circuits you may care about the signal strength of each channel. Here is an optional experiment for producing an arbitrary 8-bit signal.
• %s: No inputs; outputs 8-bit Y with channel strengths (high to low): 15 13 11 9 0 2 4 6
8-bit Analog Constant
• %s: Inputs A (8-bit) and B (8-bit). The low 3 bits of B represent a binary number (0–7); output Y (1-bit) is that bit of A, preserving signal strength.
8-bit Analog Bit Indexer
It is also configurable.
experiment.elements-plus.group.multi_bit: Multi-bit Adder
Now we will implement the addition of multi-bit binary numbers.

In the previous chapter, you already built a component that can handle the addition of one-bit binary numbers. We can recall the process of adding by columns: the carry is placed in the higher position as an addend. This also applies to binary.
In this experiment, we will build an “%s”: it takes two 8-bit binary numbers and a carry input, and outputs an 8-bit binary sum and a 1-bit carry output.
8-bit Adder
• %s: Inputs A (8-bit), B (8-bit), CI (1-bit). Treat them as binary numbers and add them, outputting the sum S (8-bit) and carry output CO (1-bit).
8-bit Adder
experiment.elements-plus.group.multiplie: Multiplier & Divider
Note: both experiments below use unsigned numbers.
A %s can multiply two numbers and output their product. Since the product of two 8-bit numbers may exceed 8 bits, the high 8 bits and the low 8 bits are output separately.
multiplier

There are usually several ways to implement a %s. Its logic can be somewhat complex, and you may skip it, but then you will not be able to build the advanced ALU. By comparison, the basic version only lacks multiplication, which does not affect the later construction of a computer architecture.
multiplier
• %s: Inputs A (8-bit) and B (8-bit); outputs Y0, containing only the low 8 bits of A*B.
Multiplier (Simple)
• %s: Inputs A (8-bit) and B (8-bit); outputs Y0 (8-bit) and Y1 (8-bit). Y0 and Y1 pack the 16-bit result of %s, where Y0 is the low 8 bits and Y1 is the high 8 bits.
Multiplier
A*B
By the congruence property of multiplication, Y0 is exactly the signed product of A and B as long as no overflow occurs.

A combinational-logic divider is theoretically possible but not recommended: its area and component count are huge, and even if you draw the circuit, it is expensive. It is better to use %s and implement it over multiple clock cycles.
sequential logic
If you want to try it, you can do the experiment below, but note that this experiment is %s: you must produce the result within the same clock cycle and cannot use sequential components.
purely combinational
• %s: Inputs A (8-bit) and B (8-bit); outputs the integer part Q (8-bit) and remainder R (8-bit) of %s.
Divider
A/B
By convention, when the divisor is 0, both Q and R output 0.
experiment.elements-plus.group.comparato: A comparator can compare two binary numbers. First, the %s.
Note: a 1-bit comparator only distinguishes zero from non-zero, so any non-zero values, such as 1 and 15, are considered equal; a non-zero value is greater than 0.

• %s: Inputs A, B, I0, and I1; outputs Y0 and Y1. When A<B, outputs Y0=15, Y1=0; when A>B, outputs Y0=0, Y1=15; when A=B, outputs Y0 and Y1 as the amplified values of I0 and I1 (15 if non-zero, otherwise 0).
Cascading the one-bit comparators above yields the %s.

• %s: Inputs A (8-bit), B (8-bit), I0 (1-bit), and I1 (1-bit); outputs Y0 (1-bit) and Y1 (1-bit). When the unsigned binary values represented by A and B satisfy A<B, outputs Y0=15, Y1=0; when A>B, outputs Y0=0, Y1=15; when A=B, outputs Y0 and Y1 as the amplified values of I0 and I1 (15 if non-zero, otherwise 0).
circuit.elements-plus.component.bit_extr: Outputs the selected bit of an 8-bit input while preserving signal strength.
circuit.elements-plus.component.bit_inde: Selects a bit of A using the low 3 bits of B and amplifies it to 0 or 15.
Selects a bit of A using the low 3 bits of B while preserving signal strength.
experiment.elements-plus.group.comparato: Inverting the sign bit introduces a fixed offset that is strictly order-preserving, so it can be used to compare signed numbers. Essentially, the sign-bit-inverted encoding is a form of “%s” corresponding to the true value of two's complement.

• %s: Inputs A (8-bit), B (8-bit), I0 (1-bit), and I1 (1-bit); outputs Y0 (1-bit) and Y1 (1-bit). When the signed binary values represented by A and B satisfy A<B, outputs Y0=15, Y1=0; when A>B, outputs Y0=0, Y1=15; when A=B, outputs Y0 and Y1 as the amplified values of I0 and I1 (15 if non-zero, otherwise 0).

There is also a comparator that compares analog signal strength. Unlike the digital 1-bit comparator, it treats signal strengths from 1 to 15 as distinct values; for example, 9 is considered greater than 8. Its implementation is relatively complex, so it is an optional experiment here.

• %s: Inputs A, B, I0, and I1; outputs Y0 and Y1. When A's signal strength is less than B's, outputs Y0=15, Y1=0; when greater, outputs Y0=0, Y1=15; when equal, outputs Y0 and Y1 as the amplified values of I0 and I1 (15 if non-zero, otherwise 0).
experiment.elements-plus.group.flip_flop: Previously we built %s. Do you remember the concept mentioned earlier: %s is a digital circuit whose output depends only on the current input state and is independent of past circuit states.
By contrast, %s is different. Its output depends not only on the current input but also on the circuit's previous state—that is, on earlier inputs.

The core of sequential logic is the %s and the %s. The clock is the unit of circuit time; one clock cycle is called a “tick”. A flip-flop is a component that, at a clock edge, determines its output from the previous tick's input.
To achieve this, we introduce a new basic component—the %s. It delays the input signal by one tick, thereby briefly storing it.

The capacitor's charge and discharge speeds can be configured; they represent the maximum signal-strength change per tick. This is usually used in analog circuits. By default, both are 15, meaning the signal will match the input immediately after one tick, with no transition.
Therefore, the capacitor itself can be seen as a flip-flop—its output depends on the previous tick's input. We call this a “D flip-flop”.
Let's try using it. In this experiment, we will build a “%s”—

• %s: Input T, output Q. When T is 0, the output at the next tick holds the current output; when T is non-zero, the output toggles (0 or 15). In other words, when the clock steps, if T is 0 the output stays unchanged; if T is non-zero the output toggles.
If the input stays non-zero, the output toggles every tick, which is exactly the expected behavior.

There is another kind that toggles only when the input changes from 0 to non-zero (previous tick 0, current tick non-zero). It can be used as a toggle switch. In redstone circuits it is often called a “T flip-flop” or “toggle latch”; here, to distinguish it, we call it a “%s”.
• %s: Input C, output Q. It toggles the output at the next tick only when C is 1 this tick and was 0 last tick; otherwise the output holds.
A capacitor can store a signal for one tick, but sometimes we want to store a signal for longer.
That is why we need a component that can preserve a signal for a long time: the register.

First, the %s. It has a write enable input. When write enable is active (non-zero), it stores the input value; when it is inactive, it holds the stored value. Note that it stores the amplified value, not the original signal strength.
• %s: Inputs A and WE, output Y. On each clock step, if WE is non-zero, Y becomes the amplified value of A; otherwise Y stays unchanged.
The 8-bit register is the 8-bit version of the same component.
• %s: Inputs A (8-bit) and WE (1-bit), output Y (8-bit). On each clock step, if WE is non-zero, Y becomes the per-lane amplified value of A; otherwise Y stays unchanged.
There is also an “%s” that can preserve analog signal strength. It is a sample-and-hold circuit that samples or holds depending on whether WE is zero.
• %s: Inputs A and WE, output Y. On each clock step, if WE is non-zero, Y becomes A's signal strength; otherwise Y stays unchanged.
experiment.elements-plus.group.multi_byt: Multi-byte Memory
A register can hold only one value at a time. When many values need to be saved and retrieved by number, a larger component is needed: %s.
memory

Memory is divided into many %s, each storing one byte (8 bits, exactly one 8-bit bus). To distinguish the cells, each one is given an %s. When accessing data, giving the address finds the corresponding cell. Memory that can access any cell directly by address is called %s (RAM).
memory cells
address
random-access memory
“Random access” here means you can access any address directly instead of searching from front to back; it has nothing to do with random numbers.
The memory components below store digital signals only. Inputs are treated as 0/non-zero, and outputs are 0 or 15; signal strength is not preserved.
First, look at the smallest %s.
4-byte RAM

• %s: inputs A (8-bit data), D (8-bit address, only the low 2 bits are valid), WE (1-bit write enable), output Y (8-bit data). It has 4 cells at addresses 0~3, corresponding to the low 2 bits of D; the upper 6 bits of D are ignored.
4-byte RAM
Its pins are:
• A (8-bit): data input, the data to write into memory;
• D (8-bit): address input, selects the memory cell to access;
• WE (1-bit): write enable, determines whether to write;
• Y (8-bit): data output, outputs the data currently stored at address D.
Its read/write rules are:

• %s: during combinational evaluation, Y directly outputs the data at address D. That is, changing D immediately changes Y; no clock step is needed. WE does not participate in address selection, and Y always outputs the data at address D.
Reads are combinational
• %s: on a clock step, if WE is non-zero, A's data is written to address D; if WE is zero, memory contents stay unchanged.
Writes are sequential

• Reads and writes use the same address D. On a clock step with WE non-zero, the data is written to address D and Y outputs the data at that address; because the write takes effect on the clock step, Y reflects the newly written value after the step.
• WE is not edge-triggered. As long as WE is non-zero on every clock step, a write occurs every tick; set WE to zero when you want to stop writing.
To use it, connect the address to D. For reads only, keep WE at 0 and take the result from Y; to write, put the data on A, make WE non-zero, step the clock, then set WE back to 0.
Expanding the capacity gives 16-byte, 64-byte, and 256-byte versions. Their pins and read/write rules are identical; only the address width differs:
• %s: the low 4 bits of D are valid, giving 16 cells at addresses 0~15;
16-byte RAM
• %s: the low 6 bits of D are valid, giving 64 cells at addresses 0~63;
64-byte RAM
• %s: all 8 bits of D are valid, giving 256 cells at addresses 0~255.
256-byte RAM
All capacities use an 8-bit address so they can share the same address bus in a circuit; for smaller capacities, simply ignore the extra high bits.

Note that RAM is %s: its contents are valid only while the circuit is running. On reset or power loss all RAM data is lost, and it is not saved with the circuit diagram or chip. RAM is therefore suitable for temporary data during program execution; use ROM or a disk for data that must persist.
volatile memory
The %s has fewer pins:
256-byte read-only memory
• D (8-bit): address input, selects the cell to read;
• Y (8-bit): data output, outputs the data stored at address D.

Unlike RAM, ROM has no WE and cannot be written while the circuit runs; it can only be read. Its contents are not runtime data but component configuration: they are written into the circuit diagram during design and are permanently preserved with the diagram or chip, surviving reset and power loss.

However, ROM is truly read-only: it cannot be erased or rewritten, and becomes immutable once compiled. The ROM contents in a compiled circuit diagram or chip are fixed; if there is a mistake, you must change the design and compile again.

Before compiling, you can double-click a ROM component in the design screen to open its editor and directly edit the 256 bytes. Since entering bytes one by one is tedious, the editor supports copying data from a disk: prepare the contents on a disk first, then import them all at once.
• %s: input D (8-bit address), output Y (8-bit data). It has 256 cells at addresses 0~255.
256-byte ROM
This experiment is optional; you can skip it for now if you do not need ROM yet.
Building a 256-byte ROM by hand is tedious, so you only need a 16-byte ROM to pass the experiment. Make its low 4 address bits valid. The contents are:
ROM contents (addresses 0~15):
When manufacturing the ROM chip itself, the required materials are multiplied by 16.
Finally, let us introduce the %s.
disk
A disk is a craftable item. Unlike the two memory components above, its data is stored in the disk item itself, not in a component in the circuit diagram.

A disk component placed in a circuit diagram is only a %s, indicating “a disk will be connected here.” The real data is stored in the disk item connected at the actual IO interface. Without a real disk item, the placeholder itself has no data.
placeholder

Once a real disk item is connected, its data survives circuit reset and power loss and can store programs and data for a long time. Compared with RAM, a disk is %s; compared with ROM, a disk can be replaced and its contents can be modified, while ROM contents are fixed after compilation.
non-volatile
You can edit disk contents in the experiment table; the ROM editor mentioned above can also copy data directly from a disk.

In the later computer architecture chapters, we will put programs and data into memory and let the computer access them by address. You will then see that the two concepts “address + data” connect computation, storage, and control.
Before building the computer architecture, let us do a small experiment that actually solves a problem with a circuit and gets us familiar with input and output.
In this experiment you need to interact with the test system through inputs and outputs, receive two numbers from the outside, add them, and output the result.

In real applications, input data is usually not immediately available, and output data cannot always be processed immediately. We therefore need a blocking input/output convention: the circuit must wait when input data is not ready, and must also wait when output data is not ready.

This chapter uses %s: a transfer is completed on the tick when VI/RI on the input side or VO/RO on the output side are both non-zero. D must be valid on that tick; it cannot be delayed to the next tick.
same-tick transfer

Specifically, when input data is ready, the outside raises VI and puts the data on DI; DI stays unchanged while VI is valid. If the circuit is ready to receive, it raises RI. The tick when VI and RI are both non-zero is the %s: the circuit saves DI into a register on that tick's clock step. Only after the transfer is complete may the outside change DI; if there is no next data for the moment, VI is withdrawn.
transfer tick

When the circuit is ready to output, it raises VO and puts the data on DO; DO stays unchanged while VO is valid. The outside raises RO when it is ready to receive. The tick when VO and RO are both non-zero is the %s: the outside reads DO before that tick's clock step. Only after the transfer is complete may the circuit withdraw VO or change DO.
transfer tick
The inputs and outputs involved in this experiment are:
Inputs:
• VI (1-bit): indicates that data is waiting to be read
• RO (1-bit): indicates that the outside is ready to read the circuit output

• DI (8-bit): input data. It stays unchanged while VI is valid; on a transfer tick where VI and RI are both non-zero, the circuit should save DI into a register at the clock step and use the saved value afterwards.
Outputs:
• VO (1-bit): indicates that there is data to output
• RI (1-bit): indicates that the circuit is ready to receive input
• DO (8-bit): output data. It stays unchanged while VO is valid; on a transfer tick where VO and RO are both non-zero, the outside reads DO before the clock step.
Input data is not necessarily ready immediately, so your circuit needs to wait until VI is valid.
In the following, V and R mean VI and RI on the input side, and VO and RO on the output side.

Only when VI and RI are both non-zero is DI actually read; likewise, only when VO and RO are both non-zero is DO actually read. D must already be valid on this %s; it cannot be delayed to the next tick.
transfer tick

%s: on the same tick, D is only required to be valid on the transfer tick; you do not have to compute the result on that tick. You may wait for data first, take several ticks to calculate, and only raise RI or VO when ready. However, after V and R are both non-zero, D cannot be delayed by another tick.
Note
For input, if VI=1 and RI=0, the outside keeps DI unchanged; for output, if VO=1 and RO=0, the circuit should keep DO unchanged. Only the tick when V and R are both non-zero completes the transfer.

The clock step is the sampling moment: DI is stable before the step and is sampled by the circuit during it; DO is read by the outside before the step, and the circuit may change it only after the step.

For example, on the input side: on tick 5, VI=1, RI=1, and DI=42. The circuit saves 42 at the clock step of tick 5 and can use the saved value from tick 6 onward; the outside changes DI to the next number only after the step of tick 5.
The output side works the same way: on tick 8, VO=1, RO=1, and DO=42. The outside reads 42 before the clock step of tick 8; only after the step of tick 8 may the circuit withdraw VO or change DO.

You may therefore decide for yourself when to be ready to receive input and when to be ready to output the result, but you cannot wait indefinitely; the test cases in this experiment have a time limit.
For this reason, we introduce a new test-case failure reason:
• %s: exceeds the maximum number of ticks allowed by the test case
TLE (Time Limit Exceeded)

Each test case must produce its output within 20 ticks. The test cases guarantee that both input values are ready within 10 ticks; after your VO becomes valid, the outside guarantees to raise RO within 2 ticks. Once output is produced, the outside immediately checks whether it is correct and moves on to the next test case.
This experiment is no longer associated with a component.

20 ticks is actually quite generous; in theory input and output can be completed in 2 ticks — read the first number on the first tick, then read the second number and output the result on the second tick. However, this cannot verify the circuit's blocking input/output behavior.

This experiment makes both input and output ready immediately, so you do not need to wait for any data. Therefore VI is 1 for both ticks, and VO should also be 1 on the second tick. RO is guaranteed to be 1 on the second tick (the same tick when VO is 1).
experiment.elements-plus.group.analog_di: This is an optional chapter. If you have trouble, you can skip it and come back later.
In the previous chapters, we usually cared only about whether a signal is present, not about its exact strength. Such circuits are called %s.

The counterpart is “%s”. Although digital signals can represent richer information and are easier to compute with, in some situations you can use analog circuits to simplify calculations. You may also need to process an input signal's strength, or output a specific strength to drive redstone devices; in those cases, this kind of circuit can be useful.

In this chapter we will convert between signal strength and binary signals. A strength of 0~15 can be represented by exactly 4 binary bits. To save component area, the 4-bit output is packed into an 8-bit bus, with only the low 4 bits valid.
• %s: Input A (1-bit), output Y (8-bit). Y is the binary representation of A's signal strength (0 maps to 0, 1 maps to 15).
• %s: Input A (8-bit), output Y (1-bit). Y's signal strength is the binary number represented by the low 4 bits of A (0 maps to 0, non-zero maps to 1; only the low 4 bits are valid).
experiment.elements-plus.group.counter.s: Next, we will build a sequential component: the counter.
When you think of a counter, you may think of cascaded %s. That is indeed a simple counter: the ripple counter.
T' flip-flops
• %s: Input C (1-bit), output Y (8-bit, binary 0/15).
8-bit Ripple Counter

On each clock step, if C changes from 0 to non-zero (0 last tick, non-zero this tick), the output starts increasing by 1, updating from the low bit to the high bit over successive ticks (so it may need up to 8 ticks to settle).
To simplify implementation, the initial state is all 15s (the inverted initial state of T' flip-flops), meaning counting starts from 255; only after the first trigger does it become 0.

This is a common simple counter in redstone circuits, but its drawbacks are obvious: it can only count up cyclically, cannot be cleared or loaded, and cannot have a custom step size, so its applications are limited. It is also far from sufficient for the architectures we will build later. In addition, as an asynchronous structure, a ripple counter needs multiple ticks to complete one count, and its inherent delay can be risky under strict timing.
A more robust solution is a synchronous counter based on registers and adders:
• %s: Inputs A (8-bit) and E (1-bit), output Y (8-bit, binary 0/15).
8-bit Addition Counter
On each clock step:
• When E is non-zero, it is in load mode: Y is set to the binary value of A;
• When E is zero, it is in increment mode: Y adds the binary value of A (wrapping on overflow).

You may also find that, with a specially configured resonator and capacitor, an analog signal can cycle from 0 to 15. This is usually not called a counter, but a %s. It is a circuit that uses the linear charging and rapid discharging of a capacitor to produce a periodic sawtooth signal strength.
sawtooth generator
• %s: No inputs, output Y. Y's signal strength cycles in one direction from 0 to 15 (returning to 0 after 15), with an initial output of 0.
Sawtooth Generator
To pass the test, you need to set the initial phase to 0. After passing, the obtained component is configurable. To learn more, see the %s chapter.
Waveform Generator
